title: Wyoming Civics (Government & Constitutions) (12th Grade)
description: Wyoming Civics (Government & Constitutions) practice - 100 questions. 70 federal civics questions plus a 30-question Wyoming layer: the Wyoming Constitution of 1890 and its structure against the U.S. Constitution, Wyoming's three branches, initiative and referendum, the Equality State firsts, and tribal sovereignty - the Eastern Shoshone and Northern Arapaho, the Wind River Indian Reservation, the 1868 Fort Bridger Treaty, the Marshall Trilogy and U.S. v. Shoshone Tribe of Indians - per W.S. 21-9-102 and standards SS12.1/SS8.1.

questions.question: A Wyoming senior reads in W.S. 21-9-102 that no diploma may be issued without passing an examination on the principles of two constitutions. The first of them, the supreme law of the whole United States, is:
questions.explanation: Wyoming's graduation examination covers the principles of the U.S. Constitution and the Wyoming Constitution. The U.S. Constitution, ratified in 1788, is the supreme law of the land - no state or federal law may override it.

questions.question: Before the Constitution took effect, the states were loosely joined under a first national framework whose Congress could request money but could not tax. That framework was:
questions.explanation: Under the Articles of Confederation (1781-1789) the central government had no power to tax or enforce its decisions, which is why delegates met in Philadelphia in 1787 to design a stronger system.

questions.question: A constitution-writing committee debates giving one official total control of lawmaking, enforcement, and judging. A member objects that concentrating all three invites tyranny. The plan the U.S. Constitution adopted instead is called:
questions.explanation: The Constitution assigns lawmaking to Congress, execution to the President, and judging to the courts. Dividing power among separate branches - an idea drawn from Montesquieu - keeps any one branch from dominating.

questions.question: The president vetoes a bill, and both chambers of Congress then pass it again with votes well above two-thirds, so it becomes law anyway. This sequence is an example of:
questions.correctAnswer: A check the legislative branch holds over the executive branch
questions.explanation: The veto override is a core check and balance: Congress may enact a law over the president's objection by a two-thirds vote of the House and the Senate.

questions.explanation: Chief Justice John Marshall's opinion in Marbury v. Madison established judicial review - the courts' power to declare laws unconstitutional - the judiciary's central check on the other branches.

questions.question: Wyoming has exactly two U.S. senators, the same number as California, even though California's population is dozens of times larger. Which constitutional arrangement produces that equality?
questions.correctAnswer: Equal representation of every state in the Senate
questions.explanation: The Connecticut Compromise gave every state equal representation in the Senate (two senators) while the House is apportioned by population. Small-population states like Wyoming benefit most from the arrangement.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: In the Senate, every state counts the same.

distractors: Each state's age as a state
questions.explanation: House seats are apportioned among the states by population after each census, with every state guaranteed at least one. Wyoming, the least populous state, has held one at-large House seat.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: House seats follow population.

questions.explanation: The Federalist Papers, written mainly by Hamilton, Madison, and Jay, argued for ratification. Federalist No. 10 and No. 51 remain classic statements on factions and checks and balances.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Federalist argued for ratification.

questions.explanation: The Bill of Rights (1791) protects freedoms such as speech, religion, and due process, and reserves unlisted powers to the states or the people.

questions.explanation: The First Amendment bars government from abridging freedom of the press and of speech, along with religion, assembly, and petition.

questions.question: Police want to search a student's home without a warrant or an emergency, and the family refuses entry. The constitutional protection the family is invoking comes from:
questions.explanation: The Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable searches and seizures and generally requires a warrant supported by probable cause.

questions.question: A defendant who cannot afford a lawyer is assigned one by the court before trial. The right to counsel in criminal cases is guaranteed by:
questions.explanation: The Sixth Amendment guarantees a speedy public trial, an impartial jury, and the assistance of counsel - applied to the states in Gideon v. Wainwright (1963).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Sixth guarantees your defense.

questions.question: A civics class sorts powers into three piles: powers granted to the national government, powers denied to it, and everything left over. Under the Tenth Amendment, the leftover powers belong to:
questions.explanation: The Tenth Amendment reserves powers not delegated to the United States, nor prohibited to the states, to the states respectively or to the people - the textual basis of federalism.

questions.question: Congress wants to regulate a new kind of business that crosses state lines, and members point to the clause letting Congress regulate commerce among the states. That clause is:
distractors: The Full Faith and Credit Clause
questions.explanation: Article I's Commerce Clause is the source of much federal regulatory power over interstate economic activity. The same clause, with its tribal counterpart, frames the federal relationship with tribal governments.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Commerce among the states - and tribes.

questions.question: A state law directly contradicts a valid federal law on the same subject, and a judge must decide which one governs. The judge applies the part of Article VI known as:
questions.explanation: The Supremacy Clause makes the Constitution, federal laws, and treaties the supreme law of the land; state law yields when the two genuinely conflict.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Federal law wins a true conflict.

questions.question: Lawmakers need a federal bank even though the Constitution never mentions banks, so they rely on the clause letting Congress make laws needed to carry out its listed powers. That is:
questions.explanation: The Necessary and Proper Clause (the 'elastic clause') lets Congress choose means to execute its enumerated powers - the basis of implied powers, confirmed in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Necessary and proper stretches the list.

questions.question: A bill has passed the House and Senate in identical form and sits on the president's desk. For it to become law by signature, the president must be acting in the role of:
questions.correctAnswer: Chief executive carrying out the lawmaking process set by Article I
questions.explanation: Article I, Section 7 sets the path: identical passage by both chambers, then presentment to the president, who may sign or veto. The president's constitutional role here is executive - the veto is the executive's check inside lawmaking.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Sign or veto - that is the choice.

questions.question: Wyoming voters elect their two senators and their one representative, but they do not directly elect the president. Their presidential preference is expressed through:
questions.correctAnswer: The Electoral College, in which Wyoming casts three electoral votes
questions.explanation: Each state's electoral votes equal its congressional delegation: Wyoming has 2 senators + 1 representative = 3 electoral votes, cast by electors chosen by the state's voters.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two plus one equals three electors.

questions.question: Midway through a term, a president resigns and the vice president takes the oath the same day. The rule that makes this succession automatic sits in:
questions.correctAnswer: Article II and the Twenty-fifth Amendment
questions.explanation: Article II provides that presidential powers and duties devolve on the vice president; the Twenty-fifth Amendment (1967) confirms the vice president becomes president and supplies procedures for disability and vacancies.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Succession is written down in advance.

questions.question: The Senate is asked to approve a treaty the president negotiated with another nation. The Constitution requires what share of senators for the treaty to take effect?
distractors: A simple majority of the House
questions.explanation: Article II gives the president power to make treaties 'by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate,' provided two-thirds of the senators present concur. Treaties - including treaties with tribal nations - then rank as supreme law.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Treaties need two-thirds of the Senate.

questions.question: A House member introduces charges that a federal official committed serious misconduct in office, and the House votes to bring those charges. The House has exercised its sole power of:
questions.explanation: The House alone may impeach (bring charges); the Senate alone tries impeachments, with conviction requiring two-thirds. Impeachment is Congress's removal check on executive and judicial officials.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The House accuses; the Senate tries.

questions.question: An official wants to know who may declare war, raise an army, and coin money. Under the Constitution, all three are powers of:
questions.explanation: Article I, Section 8 lists Congress's powers: taxing, borrowing, coining money, declaring war, and raising and supporting armies and a navy. The president commands the forces Congress raises.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The war power sits with Congress.

questions.question: A state tries to tax the mail moving through a federal post office, arguing states may tax anything inside their borders. The classic answer, from McCulloch v. Maryland, is that:
questions.correctAnswer: States may not tax the operations of the federal government
distractors: States may tax federal operations freely
Only Congress may collect any tax anywhere
Federal buildings are outside the United States
questions.explanation: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) held that 'the power to tax involves the power to destroy,' so states cannot tax federal instrumentalities; the case also upheld Congress's implied power to charter a national bank.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: States cannot tax the Union's tools.

questions.question: A defendant argues that rights not printed in the Bill of Rights were surrendered by the people when it was adopted. The amendment written to defeat exactly that reading is:
questions.explanation: The Ninth Amendment states that listing certain rights in the Constitution shall not be construed to deny or disparage others retained by the people - the list was never meant to be exhaustive.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Unlisted rights are retained, not lost.

questions.question: After the Civil War, three amendments reshaped citizenship and rights nationwide. Together the Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth are known as:
questions.explanation: The Reconstruction Amendments abolished slavery (13th), defined citizenship and guaranteed due process and equal protection against the states (14th), and barred racial discrimination in voting (15th).

questions.question: A Wyoming woman in 1920 already had years of voting behind her, but for most American women the right to vote in every state arrived with ratification of:
questions.explanation: The Nineteenth Amendment (1920) barred denying the vote on account of sex nationwide. Wyoming women had voted since 1869 under territorial law - half a century earlier.

questions.question: A state charges citizens a fee they must pay before they may vote in a federal election. The constitutional amendment that abolished that practice is:
questions.explanation: The Twenty-fourth Amendment (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections; the Supreme Court extended the ban to state elections in 1966. Barriers priced in money cannot gate the ballot.

questions.question: A popular two-term president asks whether the Constitution lets him run for a third elected term in a row. The controlling provision is:
questions.correctAnswer: The Twenty-second Amendment, which limits a president to two elected terms
questions.explanation: After Franklin D. Roosevelt's four elections, the Twenty-second Amendment (1951) limited presidents to two elected terms (plus up to two years of a predecessor's term). Wyoming's governor is likewise limited to two consecutive terms by state law.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two elected terms - that is the cap.

questions.question: Until 1913, state legislatures chose U.S. senators; after a constitutional change, voters elect them directly. That change came from:
questions.explanation: The Seventeenth Amendment (1913) moved Senate elections from state legislatures to the people, one of the Progressive Era's direct-democracy reforms.

questions.question: A proposed amendment has passed Congress by the required votes. Before it can become part of the Constitution, it must still be ratified by:
distractors: A majority of voters in a national referendum
questions.explanation: Article V requires proposal by two-thirds of Congress (or a convention) and ratification by three-fourths of the state legislatures or state conventions - the route every amendment so far has completed.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Three-fourths of states must agree.

questions.question: A class compares the two halves of the Congress: one chamber gives Wyoming the same voice as the largest state, the other gives it the smallest delegation in the building. The design, balancing state equality against population, came from:
questions.correctAnswer: The Connecticut Compromise at the Constitutional Convention
distractors: The Great Compromise of Congress in 1964
questions.explanation: The Connecticut (Great) Compromise of 1787 joined the Virginia Plan's proportional House to the New Jersey Plan's equal Senate, making ratification possible for small states like those of the interior West.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One chamber each way - the deal of 1787.

questions.question: A governor is asked to send state militia abroad under federal command and wants to know which level of government holds the war and foreign-affairs powers. In the federal system those belong to:
questions.explanation: Foreign affairs, war, immigration, and currency are national powers; states govern education, elections administration, and most day-to-day law. Tribal governments hold their own inherent sovereign authority, a third strand examined in the Wyoming layer.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Foreign affairs sit at the national level.

questions.question: When both a valid state rule and a valid federal rule can be followed at the same time, courts say the two governments are exercising their powers in a system best described as:
questions.correctAnswer: Federalism - shared and divided sovereignty between nation and states
distractors: A confederation of fully independent nations
questions.explanation: Federalism divides sovereignty: each level is supreme in its own sphere, both govern the same people, and conflicts are resolved by the Supremacy Clause only when compliance with both is impossible.

questions.question: A new senator takes office in January and a class computes how long she will serve before facing the voters again, and how that compares with a House member's cycle. The correct pairing is:
questions.correctAnswer: Senators serve six-year terms; House members serve two-year terms
distractors: Senators serve two-year terms; House members serve six-year terms
Senators serve for life; House members serve six years
questions.explanation: The Constitution staggers Senate terms at six years (one-third elected every two years) for continuity, while the whole House faces the voters every two years for responsiveness. Wyoming's two senators and single representative follow the same cycles.

questions.question: A president nominates a judge, the nominee testifies before a Senate committee, and the full Senate votes to confirm. The Senate's part of this process is its constitutional power of:
questions.explanation: Article II requires Senate confirmation for principal officers and federal judges. The president nominates; the Senate's advice-and-consent vote is the check that must follow.

questions.question: A budget fight begins, and members argue over which chamber must start any bill that raises revenue. Article I answers that revenue bills must originate in:
distractors: Either chamber equally, with no rule
questions.explanation: The Origination Clause (Article I, Section 7) requires bills for raising revenue to begin in the House - the chamber closest to the people - though the Senate may amend them.

questions.correctAnswer: The Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment
questions.explanation: Through the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause, most Bill of Rights protections have been applied ('incorporated') against state and local governments, and state procedures and substance are tested for fundamental fairness.

questions.question: A school board adopts a policy treating two groups of students differently, and a court tests the policy against the promise that no state shall deny any person the equal protection of the laws. That promise lives in:
questions.explanation: The Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment (1868) is the Constitution's central guarantee against unequal state laws - the provision behind school-desegregation and many other landmark rulings.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Equal protection is the Fourteenth's promise.

questions.correctAnswer: The Fourteenth Amendment, ratified after the Civil War
questions.explanation: Barron v. Baltimore held the Bill of Rights limited only federal action. The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) later supplied the route - its Due Process Clause - by which courts applied most of those rights against the states.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Fourteenth carried rights to the states.

questions.question: SS12.1.1.a asks Wyoming graduates to compare tribal membership on the Wind River Indian Reservation with United States citizenship. The comparison turns on the doctrine that tribal rights of self-government are:

Gifted by Congress in 1934 and revocable at will
Identical to the rights of a Wyoming county
questions.explanation: Inherent sovereignty is the core concept: tribes were self-governing long before the republic, treaties recognized rather than created that status, and tribal citizenship is a political status distinct from - and additional to - U.S. citizenship, which Congress extended to all Native Americans in 1924.

questions.question: A proposed change to the Wyoming Constitution - say, to its Declaration of Rights - cannot be made by citizen initiative or by the governor. The amendment path the constitution itself prescribes is:

questions.question: Finally, a graduate is asked why Wyoming - the least populous state - can still matter out of proportion in national civics. The answer that ties the whole course together is:
